What actually happens to your coffee after you drink it? ☕
Follow the caffeine in 3D: stomach → small intestine → liver → bloodstream → liver again → kidneys.
• Caffeine makes your stomach release more acid
• Your small intestine absorbs most of it; almost all is absorbed within about 45 minutes
• It reaches the liver first through the hepatic portal vein, and most passes right through
• Your blood carries it to your heart and up to your brain, where it blocks adenosine receptors (adenosine builds sleep pressure)
• Blood levels peak anywhere from 15 minutes to 2 hours
• Over the next hours your liver breaks it down with the enzyme CYP1A2, mostly into paraxanthine; on average half is gone in about 4–5 hours
• Your kidneys filter the leftovers into urine; only about 2–3% leaves unchanged
Save this for your next physiology exam.
3D: Digestive System by Focus Medica (Sketchfab, CC BY 4.0)
Sources: StatPearls — Caffeine; OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e (23.6); CDC Biochemical Indicators — Caffeine; EFSA — Caffeine explained; Harvard T.H. Chan Nutrition Source — Caffeine.
